defects.original:
The taxi driver offered to carry Naomi's case upstairs, but she paid him at the kerb and said the handle was stronger than it looked. It was something her mother might have said. The case had a cracked wheel and a strip of bright airline tape that seemed indecent against the bakery's pale brickwork. Across the window, someone had painted BELL & FAMILY in letters too small to conceal the old outline of BELL & SON. Naomi had helped her father scrape that window when she was seventeen. Now a stack of folded delivery trays stood where he used to keep the stool, and the bell over the door made an unfamiliar, economical click.

Ruth was alive, impatient, and kneading dough when Naomi arrived. Flour shone in the creases of her hands. She looked at the suitcase before she looked at her daughter, not from coldness, Naomi thought, but because a suitcase announced a duration that a face could conceal. A long stay required moving a chair in the upstairs room. A short stay required the careful avoidance of hope. Ruth asked whether Naomi had eaten. Naomi said she had, although the last thing she had swallowed was coffee from a paper cup outside the station. Neither of them mentioned the unanswered messages, or the envelope that had brought her home.

Daniel came through the back passage carrying his helmet. Daniel’s work card described him as a bicycle courier. The card hung from a lanyard he tucked into his sweatshirt as soon as he saw her noticing it. He had once wanted his occupation to sound temporary; now he seemed to resent questions that might make it so. He took her case without asking and carried it up the narrow stairs, bumping the cracked wheel against every second riser. The flour on those steps had become a family map: a broad pale patch where Ruth rested a sack, a narrow stripe where Daniel dragged his foot, and one spotless rectangle where the letter had lain.

The letter had arrived two days before. Their father had been dead for years, but his handwriting retained an unreasonable authority. Naomi had recognised the tilted line of the address in the photograph Daniel sent, and for a moment she had felt that familiar need to sit straighter. Daniel slipped their father’s letter into his jacket. He did it while explaining that the back window had required a new fastening, and Naomi was too occupied by the way his voice changed on the word required to stop him. Later he would remember her reaching for the envelope, not his own hand closing around it. Daniel believed Naomi still had the letter, although it was inside his own jacket and he had forgotten moving it.

They examined the repaired window after the afternoon customers had gone. Ruth had counted two hundred and forty pounds into the household tin the previous evening, putting a folded note between each group of coins as if the money might otherwise wander. The fastening cost twenty pounds, a modest sum that nevertheless acquired the weight of a family decision when Daniel read it aloud. The twenty-pound repair left two hundred and twenty pounds in the household fund. “The household fund is two hundred and twenty pounds,” Naomi said. Naomi asked whether the repair shop had supplied a receipt. Daniel put a paper on the floury table and turned it so its writing faced her, an old gesture from childhood arguments over shared homework.

Naomi set the brass key in Ruth’s palm. She had carried it on the train because Daniel said the upstairs lock sometimes caught, but now its teeth looked absurdly intimate, like something retrieved from a pocket in the wrong person's coat. Ruth closed her hand around it and said the lock caught only when someone pulled before turning. Naomi knew Ruth now held the brass key. Naomi trusted Daniel to carry the shopping, but no longer trusted his account of the family papers. That knowledge had none of the comfort of possession. She would have to knock if she went out late. Ruth would know whether she returned. The small mechanics of living together were already organising a conversation they had not yet agreed to have.

Mrs. Ames arrived with a bowl covered by a plate. Nobody could persuade her that returning home and recovering from an illness were different conditions. She placed the bowl on the counter and waited until Ruth had gone to check the oven. “Your mother has already sold the bakery,” Mrs. Ames said. She said it quietly, with the regretful certainty of someone returning a borrowed object. Naomi looked at the shop window, at the small new word FAMILY, and felt an immediate foolish anger at the painter. Mrs. Ames had heard there were papers. There was a blue tin. Someone had seen Ruth speaking to the landlord's clerk. In her account, these three observations fitted together without any uncomfortable gap.

Naomi did not ask Ruth. She had spent the journey preparing sensible questions, but they now appeared to belong to another household, one where questions did not arrive carrying accusations. Instead she helped cut bread for the evening order. The bread knife left a small cut on Naomi’s right forefinger. It was a quick, untidy injury, almost painless until Ruth ran water over it. Naomi remembered the bedsit she had rented before she left for university. Its tap had rattled in the same way, and she had washed a cut finger there while trying not to let her mother hear her crying through the telephone. She could no longer remember when she had first rented that room. What remained was the cheap blue curtain and the certainty that independence ought not to require so much explanation.

Daniel found a plaster in a drawer beneath the till. He asked whether she still played. The upright piano stood in the upstairs apartment. Naomi could see its corner through the open stairwell door, dark wood beneath an old sheet, with a bowl balanced on top to catch a leak that nobody discussed. She told him she had no room for a piano. He said that was not what he had asked. One piano key sounded a little after the others. Daniel pressed it again while looking out of the upstairs window, as if an answer might be found in the reflection rather than in the mechanism under his fingers.

Ruth called them down before Naomi could ask why he knew which key to press. A customer had ordered three loaves, collected two, and complained by telephone about the weight of the third. Ruth wanted a witness, not assistance. Naomi watched her weigh the loaf twice, the second time with Daniel checking that the scale stood clear of the wall. This was how the bakery had always defended itself: not with speeches, but with a counter cleared, a number agreed upon, a receipt produced. If the lease had been sold, the new owner would have needed both signatures. Naomi remembered that clause because their father had once explained it after a neighbour lost a business through a hurried signature. Neither adult heir had signed anything, unless Daniel had neglected to tell her far more than the price of a window fastening.

After the last delivery, Ruth took a tin from beneath the flour shelf. Ruth kept a blue tin beneath the flour shelf. It was dented at one corner and had once held biscuits Naomi was forbidden to eat before Christmas. Ruth opened it with her body between the lid and the stairs. Naomi saw paper edges, not their contents. She wanted to say she was not a child who needed shielding from a bill. Instead she asked whether there was enough tea. Ruth said there was always enough tea if people remembered where it was kept. The remark carried no obvious injury, but Naomi heard in it every year she had been away.

The letter’s envelope contained a receipt with no signature. Daniel discovered it when he finally took off his jacket and found the envelope folded against his helmet strap. Naomi read the amount but could not connect it to the repair shop. The date was older than the paper looked, and the empty signature line made her think of a promise left unacknowledged. Daniel said he would put it somewhere safe. Ruth said the blue tin was safe. Neither reached for it. For several seconds the receipt remained on the table among crumbs and a teaspoon, an ordinary scrap that had made all three of them unusually careful about moving their hands.

Naomi offered to check the accounts. Ruth said it could wait until she had rested. She planned to read every bill after breakfast. It was a plan, useful chiefly because it allowed her to postpone the fear that the bills would not explain what she wanted explained. Daniel went out to return a borrowed delivery crate. From the landing Naomi noticed light beneath the unused back-room door. Naomi could only guess why the light in the unused back room was on. It might be a timer, or a task Ruth had started before the evening rush. The light itself did not reveal a buyer, a meeting, or a secret; she reminded herself of that while doing everything possible to imagine all three.

She unpacked only what she needed for the night. The upstairs room smelled of dry wood and warm yeast rising through the floor. She placed the plaster wrapper in the bin rather than leaving it on the bedside table, a small effort to make her presence seem manageable. Below her, Ruth turned the oven dial and Daniel drew the back bolt. The sound of each action reached her clearly. Naomi stayed in the upstairs apartment after the bakery closed. She listened until the house had finished its evening arrangements and then lay down without opening her laptop. For the first time in months there was no meeting to prepare for, and she found the absence more alarming than the work. Ruth believed her children would stay for supper.

That night she dreamed her father was standing at the oven, young again. He was explaining something she could not hear because the delayed piano note kept sounding between his words. She woke before dawn to a house that contained no returning father, only a pipe settling in the wall and someone moving carefully on the stairs. She did not write the dream down as a message or an instruction. When she opened her notebook, the first thing she recorded was simpler: ask to see the register before asking who had sold the bakery. It was not forgiveness. It was the smallest honest beginning she could find. Naomi stayed in the upstairs apartment until the morning work began.

We had always defended the shop this way, by making a comparison someone else could repeat. I thought of the lease clause requiring both adult heirs' signatures. If a sale had happened, the buyer would have needed them. I had signed nothing. That made the sale an unresolved possibility rather than an event I could assume. I disliked discovering how much I wanted the rumour to explain my mother's secrecy before I had read a single page.

After the last delivery, Ruth took the blue tin from beneath the flour shelf. Its dented corner was familiar from Christmases when it had held biscuits we were forbidden to open. She stood between me and the lid. I saw the edges of papers without seeing what was written on them. I wanted to tell her I was old enough to look at a bill. I asked about tea instead. She said there was always enough if people remembered where it was kept. I heard the remark as a judgement on every year I had lived away, though she had only answered the question I chose to ask. The tin went back under the shelf before I found a better one.

Daniel took off his jacket and finally found the letter folded against his helmet strap. The discovery cleared up his mistaken belief about where he had put it. Inside its envelope was an unsigned receipt. I read the amount, but I could not connect the receipt to the repair shop. Its date looked older than the paper, and the empty line made me think of a promise nobody had acknowledged. Daniel offered to put it somewhere safe. Ruth named the blue tin. Neither reached for the paper. It lay beside crumbs and a teaspoon while all three of us acted as though moving it would answer a question. I could see the receipt clearly now and still did not know what it had paid for.

I offered to check the accounts, and Ruth said they could wait until I had rested. I planned to read every bill after breakfast. Giving the task a time let me postpone admitting that I wanted the bills to explain more than a sum. Daniel went out to return a borrowed crate. From the landing I noticed light beneath the unused back-room door. I could only guess why it was on. A timer or an unfinished job would have explained it as easily as a buyer or a meeting. I kept inventing the more troubling possibilities anyway. I stayed on the landing until I could distinguish what the light showed from what fear wanted it to show.

Upstairs I unpacked only enough for the night. The apartment smelled of dry wood and the warm yeast rising through its floor. I put the plaster wrapper in the bin, trying to make my presence look manageable. Ruth turned the oven dial below me; Daniel drew the bolt. Their actions reached me as separate familiar sounds. My mother had expected us to remain for supper, and the expectation made the room feel both welcoming and difficult to leave. I stayed in the apartment after the bakery closed, without opening the laptop I had carried all the way from the station. There was no meeting to prepare for. The absence of work unsettled me more than the work would have done.

That night I dreamed my father stood at the oven, young again. The delayed piano note interrupted everything he tried to explain. I woke before dawn to pipes settling and a careful footstep on the stairs. No returning father had made those sounds. I did not treat the dream as an instruction or add it to what I knew about the letter. In my notebook I wrote that I needed to see the register before asking who had sold the shop. The sentence did not amount to forgiveness. It was only an honest place to begin, and I found I could bear leaving it that small. I stayed in the upstairs apartment until the morning work began.
